title: Electrochemistry
objectives: Calculate oxidation numbers of elements in compounds and ions
Use changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations
Explain and use the terms redox, oxidation, reduction and disproportionation in terms of electron transfer and changes in oxidation number
Explain and use the terms oxidising agent and reducing agent
Use Roman numerals to indicate the magnitude of the oxidation number of an element
prior: Oxidation as gain of oxygen and reduction as loss of oxygen (IGCSE)
why: Batteries, rusting, bleach, photography, extracting metals and the breathalyser are all redox chemistry. Oxidation numbers are the bookkeeping tool that lets you see which atoms gain and lose electrons, balance difficult equations and name compounds. These skills appear in nearly every Paper 1 and Paper 2, in inorganic and organic questions alike.
intro: In a redox reaction, electrons move from one species to another. Oxidation numbers track where they go. This chapter covers the AS part of electrochemistry: the rules for oxidation numbers, the language of oxidising and reducing agents, disproportionation, naming compounds with Roman numerals, and balancing redox equations.

blocks.h: An oxidation number (oxidation state) is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were fully ionic, with the shared electrons given to the more electronegative atom. It is written with the sign first: +3, −2.

blocks.cap: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers (apply them in this order)
head: rule
example
rows: Na, O₂, S₈, Cl₂ are all 0
a simple ion: equal to its charge
the oxidation numbers in a compound add up to 0
the oxidation numbers in an ion add up to the charge
H is +1, except in metal hydrides (−1)
O is −2, except in peroxides (−1) and with F
Cl, Br, I are −1 unless bonded to O or F

blocks.name: oxnum
blocks.title: Oxidation number finder
blocks.h: Type a formula and choose the charge. The finder applies the rules in order and shows every step, including average values such as +8/3 in Fe₃O₄.

blocks.q: Find the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻.
blocks.err: Making the sum equal 0 instead of −2 gives +7.

blocks.h: When an element can have more than one oxidation number, its value is shown as a Roman numeral in brackets after the element (or after the ‘-ate’ ending of an anion).

blocks.q: Match each species to the oxidation number of the underlined element (the first element in each formula):
What is the oxidation number of sulfur in S₂O₃²⁻ (average value)?

blocks.cap: Two ways of describing the same change
head: in terms of electrons
in terms of oxidation number

blocks.h: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). In every redox reaction the electrons lost by one species are gained by another.
A species that accepts electrons from another species, causing it to be oxidised. The oxidising agent is itself reduced.
A species that donates electrons to another species, causing it to be reduced. The reducing agent is itself oxidised.

blocks.q: In the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
steps: Fe: +3 → +2, a decrease: Fe³⁺ is reduced
I: −1 → 0, an increase: I⁻ is oxidised
the species reduced is the oxidising agent; the species oxidised is the reducing agent
blocks.a: oxidising agent Fe³⁺; reducing agent I⁻
blocks.err: Naming the product (Fe²⁺ or I₂) instead of the reactant.

blocks.wrong: The oxidising agent is the substance that gets oxidised.
blocks.right: The oxidising agent causes oxidation, so it is itself reduced (it gains the electrons).

blocks.h: Not every atom in a redox reaction has to change. Spectator ions (and in some equations, some of the atoms of one element, as in MnO₂ + 4HCl) keep their oxidation numbers. Always check each element separately.

items: In Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, bromide ions act as the reducing agent.
A reaction in which no oxidation number changes is a redox reaction.
Redox needs a change in oxidation number (e.g. neutralisation is not redox).
Chlorine can act as a reducing agent.
With fluorine (e.g. ClF₃) chlorine is oxidised.

blocks.h: A redox reaction in which the same element in the same species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

blocks.wrong: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂ is disproportionation because one substance breaks down.
blocks.right: Here N is reduced (+5 → +3) but it is oxygen that is oxidised (−2 → 0). Two different elements change, so it is not disproportionation.

blocks.q: Is Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO a disproportionation? Explain.
blocks.a: Yes. Chlorine (0) is reduced to −1 in HCl and oxidised to +1 in HClO, both from the same species, Cl₂.

blocks.h: In a balanced redox equation the total electrons lost = total electrons gained. Oxidation numbers let you find these numbers without writing out every electron.

items: Find the elements whose oxidation numbers change, and by how much per atom.
Multiply by the number of those atoms in each formula (Cr₂O₇²⁻ has 2 Cr).
Choose multipliers so that the increase equals the decrease.
Balance the other atoms: usually O with H₂O, then H with H⁺ (in acid) or OH⁻ (in alkali).

blocks.h: A half-equation shows one species gaining or losing electrons. To combine two, multiply each so the electrons are equal, add them, and cancel anything on both sides (electrons, H⁺, H₂O).

blocks.name: balance
blocks.title: Redox balancer
blocks.h: Pick a reaction and reveal one step at a time: changes in oxidation number, half-equations, matching electrons, the final equation and a charge check.

blocks.q: Balance: MnO₄⁻ + SO₃²⁻ → MnO₂ + SO₄²⁻ (alkaline solution).
steps: 2MnO₄⁻ + 3SO₃²⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 3SO₄²⁻: O is 17 on the left and 16 on the right
Add H₂O on the left and 2OH⁻ on the right
blocks.err: Balancing atoms first and getting a correct-looking equation whose charges do not balance.

blocks.h: Moles of electrons give quick answers: moles of oxidising agent × electrons gained per formula = moles of reducing agent × electrons lost per formula.

blocks.q: How many moles of Fe²⁺ are oxidised to Fe³⁺ by 0.020 mol of MnO₄⁻ in acid?
blocks.a: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ gains 5 e⁻: 0.020 × 5 = 0.10 mol e⁻. Each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 0.10 mol Fe²⁺.

summary: Oxidation number: the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.
Elements are 0; oxidation numbers add up to 0 in a compound and to the charge in an ion.
F −1; Group 1 +1; Group 2 +2; Al +3; H +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); O −2 (−1 in peroxides, +2 in OF₂).
Roman numerals give the oxidation number: iron(III), chlorate(V), manganate(VII).
Oxidation: loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number. Reduction: gain of electrons, decrease in oxidation number.
Oxidising agent: accepts electrons and is reduced. Reducing agent: donates electrons and is oxidised.
Disproportionation: the same element in the same species is both oxidised and reduced.
Balance redox equations by making total oxidation-number increase = total decrease, then balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺ (or OH⁻).
Combine half-equations by equalising electrons, then cancel species on both sides.
Redox stoichiometry: moles of electrons lost = moles of electrons gained.

flash.q: Reduction in terms of oxidation number?

flash.a: A species that accepts electrons (and is reduced), oxidising another species
A species that donates electrons (and is oxidised), reducing another species
Redox reaction in which the same element in one species is both oxidised and reduced

flash.q: Oxidation number of an uncombined element?
Oxidation number of O in H₂O₂?
Oxidation number of H in NaH?
Oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
Oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
Oxidation number of S in SO₄²⁻?
Electrons gained per Cr₂O₇²⁻ going to Cr³⁺?

flash.a: No: N is reduced but O is oxidised

practice.q: Give the oxidation number of the named element: (a) P in H₃PO₄ (b) N in N₂H₄ (c) V in VO²⁺ (d) S in S₄O₆²⁻.
In 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, identify the species oxidised, the species reduced and the oxidising agent.
practice.a: Al is oxidised (0 → +3); Fe³⁺ in Fe₂O₃ is reduced (+3 → 0); Fe₂O₃ is the oxidising agent.

practice.q: Show that 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ is a disproportionation.
practice.a: O in H₂O₂ is −1. It goes to −2 in H₂O (reduced) and to 0 in O₂ (oxidised), all from the same species.

practice.q: Balance: Cu + NO₃⁻ + H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + NO₂ + H₂O.
practice.a: Cu loses 2; N gains 1, so 1 Cu : 2 NO₃⁻. Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + 4H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O

practice.q: 25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺(aq) reacts with 20.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄ in acid. Calculate [Fe²⁺].

practice.a: (a) iron(II) nitrate (b) potassium dichromate(VI) (c) sodium bromate(V)

assessment.q: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in HNO₃?
In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the oxidising agent is…
What is the oxidation number of oxygen in OF₂?
Which is the correct name for Na₂SO₃?
How many electrons are gained when one MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺?
In 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, which element is reduced?
Which species can act only as a reducing agent?
What is the ratio Cr₂O₇²⁻ : Fe²⁺ in their reaction in acid?
assessment.why: Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains 6 e⁻; each Fe²⁺ loses 1.

assessment.q: Which is NOT a redox reaction?
assessment.why: No oxidation number changes in the decomposition of CaCO₃.

assessment.q: The oxidation number of chlorine in ClO₄⁻ is…

assessment_s.q:
Iodine reacts with sodium thiosulfate: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.
(a) Calculate the average oxidation number of sulfur in S₂O₃²⁻ and in S₄O₆²⁻. [2]
(b) Identify the oxidising agent. Explain your answer. [2]
(c) 0.00150 mol of I₂ reacts completely. Calculate the amount of S₂O₃²⁻ used. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) S₂O₃²⁻: +2; S₄O₆²⁻: +2.5
(b) I₂; it gains electrons / its oxidation number falls from 0 to −1 (it oxidises S₂O₃²⁻)
(c) 2 × 0.00150 = 0.00300 mol

assessment_s.q:
Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide.
(a) Write the equation for the reaction. [2]
(b) Give the oxidation number of chlorine in each chlorine-containing product and name the salts formed. [2]
(c) Explain why the reaction is described as disproportionation. [1]
assessment_s.a:
(a) 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O
(b) NaCl: −1, sodium chloride; NaClO₃: +5, sodium chlorate(V)
(c) chlorine (0) in the same species is both reduced (to −1) and oxidised (to +5)

pp.skill: Finding the compound with a given oxidation number
pp.mis: Forgetting the charge on a polyatomic ion
pp.stem: In which compound does manganese have an oxidation number of +6?
pp.exp: K₂MnO₄: 2(+1) + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +6. In KMnO₄ Mn is +7, in MnO₂ +4, and in MnSO₄ +2 (sulfate is SO₄²⁻).

pp.skill: Two oxidation states within one formula
pp.mis: Accepting a fractional oxidation number as the real charge on each ion
pp.stem: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, contains three iron ions and four oxide ions in each formula unit. Iron has two different oxidation states in magnetite. What are they?
pp.exp: Total positive charge = 4 × 2 = 8 shared over three iron ions. One Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺ give 2 + 3 + 3 = 8. (The average, +8/3, is not the charge on any single ion.)

pp.skill: Average oxidation numbers of carbon
pp.mis: Ignoring hydrogen or charge when averaging
pp.stem: In which species is the average oxidation number of carbon the highest?
pp.exp: C₂O₄²⁻: 2C + 4(−2) = −2, so C = +3. CO: +2. CH₃COOH: 2C + 4(+1) + 2(−2) = 0, so average 0. C₃H₈: 3C + 8 = 0, so −8/3.

pp.skill: Spotting when an element does not change oxidation number
pp.mis: Assuming every element in a reaction changes
pp.stem: Chromium(III) oxide, Cr₂O₃, is obtained from the ore chromite, FeCr₂O₄, which contains Fe²⁺ ions. What is the change, if any, in the oxidation number of chromium?
opts: There is no change in the oxidation number.
pp.exp: In FeCr₂O₄: +2 + 2Cr + 4(−2) = 0, so Cr = +3. In Cr₂O₃: 2Cr = +6, so Cr = +3. No change.

pp.skill: Naming compounds using Roman numerals
pp.mis: Using the number of oxygen atoms instead of the oxidation number
pp.stem: What is the systematic name of KClO₄?
pp.exp: +1 + Cl + 4(−2) = 0, so Cl = +7. The Roman numeral is the oxidation number of chlorine: chlorate(VII). (KClO is chlorate(I), KClO₃ is chlorate(V).)

pp.skill: Facts about an oxidising ion
pp.mis: Adding oxidation numbers to zero for an ion
pp.stem: Which statement about the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻, is correct?
opts: It acts as an oxidising agent by gaining electrons.
The oxidation number of manganese in it is +8.
The sum of the oxidation numbers of all its atoms is zero.
It is formed when Mn²⁺ ions are reduced.
pp.exp: MnO₄⁻ oxidises other species by taking their electrons (it is itself reduced, often to Mn²⁺). Mn + 4(−2) = −1, so Mn = +7. The oxidation numbers add up to the charge, −1. Making MnO₄⁻ from Mn²⁺ is an oxidation.

pp.skill: Describing reduction of an oxidising agent in electron terms
pp.mis: Mixing up gain and loss of electrons
pp.stem: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions. Which statement about the manganese is correct?
opts: Each Mn atom loses 5 electrons and is oxidised.
Each Mn atom gains 5 electrons and is reduced to Mn²⁺.
Each Mn atom gains 1 electron and is reduced to Mn⁶⁺.
The oxidation number of Mn does not change.
pp.exp: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Mn goes from +7 to +2: it gains 5 electrons, so it is reduced. (Each Fe²⁺ loses one electron.)

pp.skill: One element oxidised and reduced in the same reaction
pp.mis: Treating the two copper species as unchanged
pp.stem: Copper metal reacts with copper(II) chloride solution: Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → 2CuCl(s). Which statement is correct?
opts: Copper is both oxidised and reduced.
Copper is neither oxidised nor reduced.
pp.exp: Cu(0) → Cu(+1) in CuCl: oxidised. Cu²⁺(+2) → Cu(+1): reduced. Two different copper species meet at the same oxidation state. (This is the reverse of disproportionation, sometimes called comproportionation.)

pp.skill: Which elements are oxidised in a roasting reaction
pp.mis: Not checking every element
pp.stem: Iron pyrite, FeS₂, contains Fe²⁺ and S₂²⁻ ions. It is roasted in air: 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂. Which elements are oxidised?
pp.exp: Fe: +2 → +3 (oxidised). S: −1 → +4 (oxidised). O: 0 → −2 (reduced).

pp.skill: Spectator and reducing roles of the same ion
pp.mis: Assuming every ion of one type plays the same role
pp.stem:
MnO₂(s) + 4HCl(aq) → MnCl₂(aq) + Cl₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
Which statement about this reaction is correct?
opts: All the chloride ions act as reducing agents.
Only half of the chloride ions act as reducing agents.
MnO₂ acts as a reducing agent.
The H⁺ ions act as oxidising agents.
pp.exp: Of the 4 Cl⁻, two are oxidised to Cl₂ (reducing agents) and two stay as Cl⁻ in MnCl₂. Mn goes from +4 to +2, so MnO₂ is the oxidising agent. H stays +1.

pp.skill: Recognising an unusual role for an element
pp.mis: Assuming a halogen is always the oxidising agent
pp.stem: In which reaction does chlorine act as a reducing agent?
pp.exp: In ClF₃ chlorine is +3 (F is always −1), so chlorine is oxidised and gives electrons to fluorine: it is the reducing agent. In A, B and D chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (oxidising agent).

pp.skill: Roles of hydrogen peroxide in different reactions
pp.mis: Not tracking the oxidation number of O
pp.stem:
Three reactions of hydrogen peroxide are shown.
1 H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O
2 H₂O₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl + O₂
3 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
In which reaction does H₂O₂ act only as a reducing agent?
pp.exp: O in H₂O₂ is −1. In 2 it goes to 0 in O₂ (oxidised), so H₂O₂ is the reducing agent. In 1 it goes to −2 (oxidising agent). In 3 it does both (disproportionation).

pp.skill: Classifying a reaction using oxidation numbers
pp.mis: Calling any reaction of one element in two states disproportionation
pp.stem: Sodium hydride reacts with water: NaH + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. NaH contains Na⁺ and H⁻ ions. How is this reaction classified?
pp.exp: H in H⁻ (−1) is oxidised to 0; one H in H₂O (+1) is reduced to 0. It is a redox reaction. It is not disproportionation, because the hydrogen comes from two different species.

pp.skill: Redox catalysis by an ion that changes oxidation state
pp.mis: Confusing which species is oxidised and which reduced
pp.stem:
Iron ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate and iodide ions.
step 1: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺
step 2: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂
Which statement is correct?
opts: Fe²⁺ ions are regenerated in step 2, so iron ions act as a catalyst.
Fe³⁺ ions act as a reducing agent in step 2.
I⁻ ions act as an oxidising agent in step 2.
S₂O₈²⁻ ions are oxidised in step 1.
pp.exp: Fe²⁺ used in step 1 is remade in step 2, so the iron is not used up: a catalyst. In step 2 Fe³⁺ gains electrons (oxidising agent) and I⁻ loses them (reducing agent). S₂O₈²⁻ gains electrons in step 1: it is reduced.

pp.skill: Identifying disproportionation
pp.mis: Choosing any decomposition in which one element is reduced
pp.stem: Which reaction is an example of disproportionation?
pp.exp: Disproportionation: the same species is both oxidised and reduced. Cu(+1) → Cu(0) and Cu(+2). In C, N is reduced but O is oxidised (two elements). B is not redox. D is a displacement.

pp.skill: Statements about a disproportionation
pp.mis: Thinking water is the oxidising agent
pp.stem: Chlorine reacts with water: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO. Which statement is correct?
opts: Water acts as an oxidising agent.
The oxidation number of hydrogen increases.
pp.exp: Cl goes from 0 to −1 (in HCl) and to +1 (in HClO): the same element is both reduced and oxidised. H stays +1 and O stays −2.

pp.skill: Disproportionation and the oxidation number in a product
pp.mis: Miscounting oxygen in the chlorate ion
pp.stem: On heating, potassium chlorate(I) reacts: 3KClO → 2KCl + KClO₃. Which row is correct?
opts: disproportionation: yes; oxidation number of Cl in KClO₃: +5
disproportionation: yes; oxidation number of Cl in KClO₃: +3
disproportionation: no; oxidation number of Cl in KClO₃: +5
disproportionation: no; oxidation number of Cl in KClO₃: +6
pp.exp: Cl in KClO is +1. It goes to −1 (KCl) and +5 (KClO₃): disproportionation.

pp.skill: Comparing three bromine reactions
pp.mis: Calling a displacement reaction disproportionation
pp.stem:
Three reactions are shown.
1 2KBrO₃ → 2KBr + 3O₂
2 3Br₂ + 6KOH → 5KBr + KBrO₃ + 3H₂O
3 Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂
Which statement is correct?
opts: Reaction 1 is not a redox reaction.
pp.exp: 2: Br₂ (0) → Br⁻ (−1) and BrO₃⁻ (+5): disproportionation. 1 is redox (Br +5 → −1, O −2 → 0). KBrO₃ is bromate(V). In 3 bromine is reduced.

pp.skill: Balancing a disproportionation by electron count
pp.mis: Balancing atoms but not electrons
pp.stem: In acidic solution, W mol of manganate(VI) ions, MnO₄²⁻, disproportionate to give U mol of MnO₄⁻ and V mol of MnO₂. Manganese is the only element that changes oxidation number. What are W, U and V?
pp.exp: Mn: +6 → +7 (loses 1 e⁻) and +6 → +4 (gains 2 e⁻). Electrons balance with 2 MnO₄⁻ for each MnO₂: 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O.

pp.skill: Size of a change in oxidation number
pp.mis: Comparing the starting values rather than the changes
pp.stem: In which reaction does the oxidation number of nitrogen change by the largest amount?
pp.exp: C: −3 → +2, a change of 5. A: −3 → +1 and +5 → +1 (changes of 4). B: +2 → +4 (2). D: +4 → +4 (no change).

pp.skill: Largest increase using average oxidation numbers
pp.mis: Not using average values for S in S₂O₃²⁻ and S₄O₆²⁻
pp.stem: Use average oxidation numbers where needed. In which reaction does the named element show the largest increase in oxidation number?
opts: chlorine in Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O

pp.skill: Balancing a redox equation using electrons
pp.mis: Forgetting that Cr₂O₇²⁻ contains two Cr atoms
pp.stem:
...X... Cr₂O₇²⁻ + ... Fe²⁺ + ... H⁺ → ... Cr³⁺ + ...Y... Fe³⁺ + ... H₂O
What are X and Y when the equation is balanced with the smallest whole numbers?
pp.exp: Each Cr goes +6 → +3 (gains 3), so one Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains 6 electrons. Each Fe²⁺ loses 1. So 1 Cr₂O₇²⁻ : 6 Fe²⁺: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O.

pp.skill: Mole ratio from changes in oxidation number
pp.mis: Inverting the ratio
pp.stem: In acidic solution, iodate(V) ions, IO₃⁻, oxidise iodide ions to iodine. The iodate(V) ions are also converted to iodine. What is the ratio IO₃⁻ : I⁻ in the balanced equation?
pp.exp: I in IO₃⁻: +5 → 0 (gains 5). Each I⁻: −1 → 0 (loses 1). So 1 IO₃⁻ : 5 I⁻: IO₃⁻ + 5I⁻ + 6H⁺ → 3I₂ + 3H₂O.

pp.skill: Redox stoichiometry from oxidation numbers
pp.mis: Counting one Cr per dichromate ion
pp.stem: In acidic solution, Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺. How many moles of Sn²⁺ can be oxidised to Sn⁴⁺ by 0.50 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻?
pp.exp: 0.50 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains 0.50 × 6 = 3.0 mol electrons. Each Sn²⁺ loses 2, so 3.0 / 2 = 1.5 mol Sn²⁺.

pp.skill: Moles of product from electron transfer
pp.mis: Using 1 electron per Cl₂ instead of 2
pp.stem: Potassium manganate(VII) reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to give MnCl₂ and chlorine. Only Mn and Cl change oxidation number. How many moles of Cl₂ are produced from 1.0 mol of KMnO₄ and an excess of HCl?
pp.exp: Mn: +7 → +2, so 1.0 mol KMnO₄ accepts 5.0 mol electrons. Each Cl₂ formed releases 2 electrons (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻), so 5.0 / 2 = 2.5 mol Cl₂.

pp.skill: Deducing a product’s oxidation number from a reacting ratio
pp.mis: Forgetting the nitrate ions that are not reduced
pp.stem: When zinc dissolves in dilute HNO₃ the products are Zn(NO₃)₂, H₂O and a single nitrogen oxide. The reacting ratio is Zn : HNO₃ = 2 : 5. Deduce the oxidation number of N in that oxide.
pp.exp: 4 Zn lose 8 electrons. 8 of the 10 HNO₃ end up as nitrate in 4Zn(NO₃)₂, so 2 N atoms are reduced, each gaining 4 electrons: +5 → +1. The oxide is N₂O: 4Zn + 10HNO₃ → 4Zn(NO₃)₂ + N₂O + 5H₂O.

pp.skill: Identifying a reactant from redox stoichiometry
pp.mis: Not checking that the electrons balance
pp.stem: One mole of a vanadium oxide, X, reacts exactly with 5 mol of magnesium. The only products are 2 mol of vanadium metal and magnesium oxide. Only V and Mg change oxidation number. What is X?
pp.exp: 5 Mg lose 10 electrons; 2 V atoms gain them, so each V gains 5: it started as +5. X contains 2 V, so it is V₂O₅.

pp.skill: Balancing a full equation using oxidation numbers
pp.mis: Balancing O before electrons
pp.stem:
Sulfur reacts with concentrated nitric acid.
aS + bHNO₃ → cH₂SO₄ + dNO₂ + eH₂O
a to e are the smallest whole numbers. What is a + b + c + d + e?
pp.exp: S: 0 → +6 (loses 6). N: +5 → +4 (gains 1). So 1 S : 6 HNO₃: S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 6NO₂ + 2H₂O. Sum = 1 + 6 + 1 + 6 + 2 = 16.

pp.skill: Balancing a disproportionation of phosphorus
pp.mis: Splitting the electrons equally between products
pp.stem:
White phosphorus reacts with hot sodium hydroxide solution.
P₄ + xNaOH + yH₂O → zNaH₂PO₂ + PH₃
What are x, y and z?
pp.exp: P: 0 → +1 in NaH₂PO₂ (loses 1) and 0 → −3 in PH₃ (gains 3). So 3 P go to NaH₂PO₂ and 1 P to PH₃. Then Na: x = 3; H: 3 + 2y = 6 + 3, so y = 3.

pp.skill: Combining half-equations to find reacting moles
pp.mis: Using the moles in a half-equation directly
pp.stem:
Ammonia removes NO from power-station exhaust, forming nitrogen.
2NH₃ → N₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻
2NO + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → N₂ + 2H₂O
How many moles of NH₃ are needed for each mole of N₂ produced overall?
pp.exp: Balance electrons: 2 × (first) gives 12 e⁻; 3 × (second) takes 12 e⁻. Overall: 4NH₃ + 6NO → 5N₂ + 6H₂O. So 4 mol NH₃ give 5 mol N₂: 0.8 mol NH₃ per mol N₂.

pp.skill: Half-equations, oxidation numbers and the overall ionic equation
pp.stem:
Acidified manganate(VII) ions oxidise ethanedioic acid, H₂C₂O₄, to carbon dioxide.
half-equation 1: H₂C₂O₄ → 2CO₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻

parts.q: Identify the species that is reduced. Explain your answer.
Calculate the oxidation number of carbon in H₂C₂O₄ and in CO₂.
ms: +3 in H₂C₂O₄ and +4 in CO₂ (both needed)

parts.q: Construct the ionic equation for the reaction.
ms: multiply by 5 and 2 so that 10 electrons cancel

pp.skill: Oxidation numbers and electron transfer in a test reaction
pp.stem:
Nitrite ions can be detected by warming with zinc in alkali. Ammonia is given off.
NO₂⁻ + 3Zn + 5OH⁻ + 5H₂O → NH₃ + 3[Zn(OH)₄]²⁻

parts.q: Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in NO₂⁻ and in NH₃.
Identify the species that is oxidised. Explain your answer in terms of electrons.
Show that the electrons transferred balance in this equation.
ms: 3 Zn lose 3 × 2 = 6 electrons; one N gains 6 electrons (+3 → −3)

pp.skill: Equations, oxidation numbers and the reducing agent
pp.stem: This question is about two redox reactions.

parts.q: Magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide and a gas that burns with a squeaky pop. Write the equation and state which species is reduced.
MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. Deduce the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₂ and in MnCl₂.
Identify the reducing agent in this reaction.

ms: a species that accepts electrons (and is itself reduced), causing another species to be oxidised

pp.skill: Oxidation numbers and systematic names
pp.stem: Oxidation numbers help to name compounds and track redox changes.

parts.q: Give the oxidation number of nitrogen in each species: N₂O, NO₂, HNO₃, NH₄⁺.
ms: HNO₃ +5; NH₄⁺ −3 (all four for 2 marks, two or three for 1)

parts.q: Calcium phosphide, Ca₃P₂, is an ionic solid. Deduce the oxidation numbers of calcium and phosphorus in it.
Name these compounds using oxidation numbers: Fe₂(SO₄)₃, KClO₃, NaNO₂.
ms: potassium chlorate(V) and sodium nitrate(III) (both needed)
